analysis.one_liner: Bans companies from forcing consumers to settle disputes in private arbitration instead of court.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have barred companies from forcing consumers into arbitration, was referred to the House Financial Services Committee in February 2009 and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Most consumer contracts — for credit cards, loans, phones, and other goods and services — contain a clause requiring disputes to be settled by a private arbitrator chosen under the company's process, rather than in court, and the consumer cannot sign up for the service without accepting it. This bill would make those clauses unenforceable and treat them as an unfair and deceptive trade practice, letting consumers sue in court instead. It would still allow arbitration if both sides agree to it after a dispute has already arisen [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers — anyone who signs a credit card agreement, phone contract, or other standard-form consumer contract. If it passed, they could take disputes over fees, billing, or broken promises to court, and could join class actions, instead of being funneled into a private arbitration process chosen by the company. Because the bill covers any individual in a consumer transaction, the benefit reaches essentially everyone [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers with arbitration clauses in contracts

how_it_helps.text: It would make any written contract term requiring binding arbitration in a consumer transaction unenforceable and an unfair and deceptive trade practice under federal or state law [S3].

It would apply to the full range of consumer dealings — goods, services, real property, credit, and financial products — so disputes could go to court instead of a private arbitration process chosen by the company [S3].
It would still let two parties agree to arbitration after a dispute has actually arisen, when the consumer knows what they are agreeing to [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Companies that write consumer contracts — banks, credit card issuers, retailers, and service providers — would lose a tool that keeps consumer disputes out of court, where class actions and public court records can be costly and expose business practices to scrutiny [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill still allows binding arbitration if both parties agree to it in writing after a dispute has arisen [S3], so it bans only pre-dispute clauses rather than arbitration itself.

Companies argue arbitration is faster and cheaper than court for resolving disputes, and that banning it would raise their litigation costs and potentially the cost of credit and other consumer products [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to consumers is substantial: court access is the practical way to challenge wrongful fees, collections, and discrimination, and forced arbitration has effectively shut that door for most consumer contracts [S2][S3]. The main cost falls on companies, who would face more lawsuits and could pass some of those costs to consumers; a good-faith objection is that arbitration can be faster and cheaper than court in some cases, which is why the bill still allowed arbitration when both sides agree after a dispute arises [S2]. The bill does not address quality of the courts themselves, so its value depends on litigation being a workable remedy.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Financial Services Committee in February 2009, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Luis Gutierrez introduced the bill on February 11, 2009 [S1][S5].
The House referred it to the Committee on Financial Services the same day [S5].
No further action was taken — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — through the end of the 111th Congress [S5].
The bill drew no cosponsors, so no other member of the House publicly backed it [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks, credit card issuers, and other companies that put mandatory arbitration clauses in their consumer contracts kept the ability to push disputes into private arbitration.

for.name: Rep. Luis Gutierrez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never took it up — no hearing, no markup, no vote

against.name: Financial services industry
against.role: Credit card issuers, lenders, and retailers using arbitration clauses
against.what_they_did: Opposed restrictions on mandatory arbitration clauses during this era, when such clauses were standard in consumer contracts

sides.party_line_note: The bill never advanced far enough for any recorded votes, and no other member cosponsored it, so the partisan shape of support or opposition is unknown.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers and consumer lenders
industries.note: These companies rely heavily on mandatory arbitration clauses in their contracts to keep disputes out of court, including disputes over fees and lending practices. The bill would make those clauses unenforceable and expose them to consumer class actions and lawsuits.

industries.industry: Retailers and other sellers of goods and services
industries.note: Any business using standardized consumer contracts with arbitration clauses would have to drop them and face ordinary court claims from customers.
Private arbitration providers charge fees for consumer disputes; banning mandatory clauses would shrink this business.
